name: JavaFX

beginner.content:
What is JavaFX?

• JavaFX is Java's modern toolkit for building desktop GUI applications, and is the successor to the older Swing/AWT toolkits.
• A JavaFX app is structured around three core concepts:
1. Stage - the top-level window (like a JFrame in Swing).
2. Scene - the content container placed inside a Stage.
3. Scene Graph - a tree of Nodes (buttons, labels, layouts) that make up the Scene's content.
• Every JavaFX application extends the Application class and overrides start(Stage primaryStage).

Fresher Notes

  • JavaFX is the modern Java toolkit for desktop GUI applications, replacing Swing for new projects.
  • An app extends Application and builds its UI in start(Stage); launch() starts it.
  • The UI is a tree of nodes (a scene graph) inside a Scene on a Stage (the window).

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

JavaFX renders through a scene graph managed on a single UI thread, the JavaFX Application Thread. A pulse (about 60 per second) synchronizes the scene graph with the render thread: dirty nodes are updated, layout runs, CSS is applied, and the result is drawn with hardware acceleration when available. Anything that blocks the Application Thread delays pulses and freezes the UI.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to build UI: pure Java code, FXML with Scene Builder, and mixed approaches. Ways to run: Application.launch, Maven or Gradle plugins, jlink runtime images, jpackage installers. Modules: javafx.base, controls, graphics, fxml, media, web, swing.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • JavaFX is distributed separately from the JDK (OpenJFX); add the modules javafx.controls and others to the project.
  • Layouts (VBox, HBox, BorderPane, GridPane) arrange nodes; controls (Button, TextField, TableView) provide behaviour.
  • Styling uses CSS and UI can be declared in FXML with a controller.

Senior Notes

  • Keep long work off the JavaFX Application Thread (use Task/Service) or the UI freezes.
  • Use properties and bindings to keep UI and model in sync without manual listeners.
  • Package with jlink/jpackage to ship a runtime with the application.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes: updating the UI from background threads (IllegalStateException), doing blocking I/O in handlers, missing module opens for FXML reflection, forgetting Platform.exit (threads keep the JVM alive) and shipping without the native libraries. Use Task/Service and the correct module declarations.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: keep the scene graph small, use virtualized controls, avoid layout thrash (many resize/relayout cycles), cache static nodes (setCache(true)), and keep CSS simple. Profile with the JavaFX pulse logger.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a small desktop client that talks to a REST API. The UI shows a table, loads data in a Task, shows a progress indicator and handles errors in a dialog.

beginner.content:
Understanding the Scene Graph

The scene graph is a hierarchical tree of Node objects. Container nodes (like VBox, HBox) can hold child nodes, forming a parent-child tree - similar in spirit to the DOM in a web page. Each node can only appear ONCE in the scene graph at a time.

Fresher Notes

  • The scene graph is a tree: the root node contains child nodes, which may contain more nodes. Layout panes and controls are nodes.
  • A Stage shows one Scene; replacing the scene root changes the screen.
  • Lifecycle of an Application: init(), start(Stage), stop().

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Building a scene graph in code.

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Every node has a parent (except the root), transforms relative to it, bounds in several coordinate systems (layout, local, parent) and a render state. Changing a property marks the node dirty; on the next pulse JavaFX recomputes layout (top-down for size, bottom-up for preferred sizes), applies CSS and synchronizes with the renderer.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tree operations: add, remove, reorder (toFront), find by id (lookup("#id")), traverse children, apply CSS classes and pseudo-classes, set clip, effects and transforms. Lifecycle hooks: sceneProperty() listeners and Application.stop().

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Nodes have properties: position, size, visibility, opacity, transforms, effects and CSS classes.
  • Group, Pane and layout containers manage children; getChildren().add() modifies the tree.
  • Events bubble through the tree; filters and handlers can intercept them.

Senior Notes

  • Keep the scene graph small: thousands of nodes slow rendering; use virtualized controls (ListView, TableView) for big data.
  • Modify the graph only on the Application Thread; other threads must use Platform.runLater.
  • Clean up listeners and bindings in stop() or when removing nodes to avoid leaks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: leaving old nodes referenced by listeners (leaks), building a huge static graph for long lists, modifying the children list while iterating it, and relying on node sizes before layout has run. Use virtualization and listen for layout bounds changes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Rendering cost scales with node count and effects. Cache complex static nodes, avoid large blur or shadow effects on animated nodes, and use Canvas for very many simple primitives.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a dashboard with tiles. Each tile is a small component node; tiles are added and removed as widgets are configured, and all listeners are removed when a tile is closed.

beginner.content:
Common Layout Panes

JavaFX ships several layout containers that automatically arrange their children:
• VBox / HBox - vertical / horizontal stacking.
• BorderPane - top, bottom, left, right, and center regions.
• GridPane - rows and columns, like an HTML table.
• StackPane - layers children on top of one another (centered by default).

Fresher Notes

  • Layout panes position children: VBox (vertical), HBox (horizontal), BorderPane (five regions), GridPane (rows and columns), StackPane (layers), FlowPane.
  • Common controls: Label, Button, TextField, CheckBox, ComboBox, ListView, TableView.
  • Set spacing, padding and alignment to make layouts readable.

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A Region calculates three sizes: minimum, preferred and maximum. A parent asks each child for its preferred size, gives it space according to constraints (grow/shrink priorities, alignment, margins), then calls layout recursively. This is why layouts adapt when the window resizes or content changes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Panes: VBox/HBox, BorderPane, GridPane (row/column spans and constraints), StackPane, FlowPane, TilePane, AnchorPane, SplitPane, TabPane, ScrollPane. Controls: ListView, TableView, TreeView, ComboBox, DatePicker, Spinner, Slider.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Use constraints: HBox.setHgrow, GridPane.setConstraints, ColumnConstraints for percentage widths.
  • TableView needs TableColumn with cell value factories bound to model properties.
  • Style with CSS: node.getStyleClass().add("primary") and a stylesheet.

Senior Notes

  • Responsive layouts: let panes grow (Priority.ALWAYS) and avoid fixed pixel sizes.
  • Use FXML plus a controller for larger screens; separate layout from logic.
  • Prefer ObservableList with TableView/ListView so changes update automatically.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: fixed pixel sizes (breaks on high-DPI or resize), nesting many panes needlessly, blocking the UI while populating a TableView with a huge list, and forgetting cell factories for custom rendering. Let panes grow, keep nesting shallow and use cell factories.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

TableView and ListView virtualize cells: only visible rows are created. Keep cell updateItem cheap (no I/O), use properties, and apply sorting/filtering with SortedList and FilteredList over the observable list.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an order entry screen using FXML for structure, a controller for logic, CSS for theming, and validation that enables the Save button only when the form is valid.

beginner.content:
Handling User Events

JavaFX controls expose setOn<EventType>() methods to attach an event handler - most commonly implemented with a lambda expression since Java 8.

Fresher Notes

  • Events notify your code about user actions: clicks, key presses, mouse moves. Register handlers such as setOnAction, setOnKeyPressed, setOnMouseClicked.
  • Handlers are usually lambdas that receive the event object.
  • Handlers run on the JavaFX Application Thread, so keep them fast.

Worked Example 1

Event filter that consumes.

Worked Example 2

Binding instead of listener.

Practice Exercise 1

Click and key handlers.

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

When you click, JavaFX picks the target node by hit testing, builds the event dispatch chain from the scene root to the target, runs event filters on the way down (capture), then handlers on the way back up (bubble). Handlers run on the Application Thread. A consumed event stops further propagation.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Event types: ActionEvent, MouseEvent, KeyEvent, ScrollEvent, TouchEvent, DragEvent, WindowEvent, plus custom events. Tools: setOnXxx convenience methods, addEventHandler/Filter, accelerators (scene.getAccelerators()), drag and drop, property listeners and bindings.

intermediate.content:
Property Binding

JavaFX controls expose their state as Property objects (e.g. textProperty()). Binding one property to another keeps them automatically synchronized - no manual event-listener wiring needed.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Event flow: capturing (filters, root to target) then bubbling (handlers, target to root); call event.consume() to stop propagation.
  • Use addEventHandler and addEventFilter for multiple or generic handlers.
  • Properties support change listeners: textProperty().addListener((obs, old, val) -> ...).

Senior Notes

  • Do not perform blocking work in handlers; start a Task and update the UI when it finishes.
  • Remove listeners you add to long-lived properties to prevent memory leaks.
  • Prefer bindings over manual listeners for simple one-way synchronization.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: blocking handlers, forgetting to remove listeners from long-lived objects, doing UI changes from non-UI threads, anonymous classes capturing the enclosing window, and handlers that throw (the exception ends in the default handler). Use Tasks, remove listeners and handle exceptions.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Event handling cost is small, but handlers that trigger layout (changing text and sizes repeatedly) or rebuild large parts of the scene are expensive. Batch updates, debounce frequent events such as typing or resizing.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a form with validation feedback. Property listeners validate on change, a binding enables the submit button, and the submit handler runs the network call in a Task with progress and error handling.

cheatNotes: Application - Base class every JavaFX app extends
start(Stage) - Entry point method JavaFX calls after launch()
Stage - The top-level window of a JavaFX application
Scene - The container of content placed inside a Stage
Scene Graph - Tree of Node objects that make up a Scene's visual content
Node - Base class for anything visual: buttons, labels, panes, shapes
VBox / HBox - Stack children vertically / horizontally
GridPane - Row-and-column layout, like an HTML table
StackPane - Layers children on top of each other
setOnAction() - Attaches a click handler to a control like Button
Property (e.g. textProperty()) - Observable, bindable wrapper around a value
bind() - Keeps one property automatically synced with another
FXML - XML-based markup for declaring JavaFX UIs separately from Java code
CSS styling - JavaFX supports CSS stylesheets for theming controls
launch(args) - Bootstraps the JavaFX runtime and calls start()
Platform.runLater() - Schedules code to run on the JavaFX Application Thread
